title: Top-down design: from requirements to functions
lead: Complex software becomes easier to build and verify when decomposed into small operations with clear responsibilities.
why: Decomposition supports large projects: define responsibilities first, implement and test each part, then verify the complete behavior.
objectives: Decompose a requirement into cohesive functions.
Specify function inputs, outputs and constraints.
Separate input validation, computation and presentation.
Use unit-level and integration-level test cases.
prerequisites: You can describe control flow in a diagram.
Arithmetic is enough; function syntax is explained through examples.

concepts.definition: Breaking a large problem into smaller problems with explicit boundaries.
A named operation that receives arguments and can return a result.
The expected inputs, outputs and valid calling conditions.
How closely a component's responsibilities belong together.

sections.title: Start with the result the user needs
paragraphs: An order calculator can be described as: read input → validate → calculate → report. Instead of writing one long main, state the responsibility of each stage.
At a lower level, calculation splits into a subtotal and a discount operation. Validation enforces nonnegative values and a percentage between 0 and 100.

sections.title: Define contracts before implementation details
paragraphs: subtotal(price,qty) computes a total under an explicit valid-input assumption. valid returns true or false for the specified bounds.
Choose names that express purpose: subtotal is more helpful than doStuff. A reporting function need not know the internals of the calculation.

sections.title: Separate calculation from interaction
paragraphs: std::cin and std::cout belong at the application boundary. Computation functions should ideally not be tied to console interaction so the same logic can serve a UI or test.
valid and subtotal can then be examined independently. This reduces diagnostic complexity without replacing end-to-end tests.

sections.title: Manage dependencies
paragraphs: Higher-level orchestration calls lower-level functions. When each component receives only necessary arguments, changes are more localized and tests become focused.
In the example, main handles user input but subtotal does not. This separation is a reusable architecture principle.

sections.title: Diagnose a multi-step calculation
paragraphs: If a total is wrong, check input validation, intermediate subtotal and discount calculation in sequence. Each boundary has observable values.
For teaching we use int; professional monetary systems need explicit units, overflow policies and rounding conventions. Those are later topics in the curriculum.

workedExamples.purpose: valid and subtotal have distinct jobs.
steps: valid checks whether the inputs are acceptable.
Each function can be tested separately.

experiments.title: Zero discount
experiments.verification: Check that the discount function has no effect at 0%.

experiments.title: Invalid percentage
experiments.prediction: valid rejects it; output is invalid.
experiments.verification: Do not mix validation and arithmetic.

diagnostics.symptom: A calculation function prints an error directly
diagnostics.cause: Business logic and presentation have been coupled.
diagnostics.fix: Return a value or status and print from main.

diagnostics.symptom: Applying discounts early changes the total
diagnostics.cause: The order of operations and rounding policy are unclear.
diagnostics.fix: Define the rounding rule before choosing an evaluation order.

assessment.question: Why separate a pure calculation from I/O?
answers: It becomes easier to test and reuse
It hides it from the compiler
assessment.explanation: Computation then remains independent of the user interface.

assessment.question: What does valid do?
assessment.explanation: Its contract is about valid arguments.

assessment.question: What is a useful decomposition?
answers: Small functions with explicit roles and contracts
